pool.text: French admiral Édouard Bouët-Willaumez negotiated a trade and protection treaty with local Mpongwé ruler Antchoué Komé Rapontcombo.
American missionaries from New England established a mission in Baraka, Gabon, on the site of Libreville.
The Brazilian slave ship L'Elizia, carrying slaves from the Congo, was captured near Loango by the French navy.
Fifty-two of the freed slaves were resettled on the site of Libreville, which means Freetown in French.
Libreville became the administrative capital of France's Congo-Gabon colony.
Gabon became part of French Equatorial Africa, also known as Afrique équatoriale française.
Paris-based Banque de l'Afrique Occidentale opened the first bank branch in Libreville.
Libreville was the central focus of the Battle of Gabon involving Free French forces.
Léon M'ba won Libreville's first free mayoral election with national independence approaching.
Société des Brasseries du Gabon was founded under the impetus of the French industrialist Pierre Castel.
The hosting of the Organisation of African Unity summit drove a first wave of prestige construction.
The Trans-Gabon Railway between Owendo and Franceville was completed.
The Banque de Paris et des Pays-Bas Gabon adopted its current name as a private multinational.
The Plan Stratégique Gabon Émergent placed Libreville and its suburbs at the centre of an industrial strategy.
Moov Africa Gabon Telecom was formed by the merger of Gabon Telecom and Moov Gabon.
The GSEZ Mineral Port was inaugurated as a dedicated bulk terminal primarily for manganese ore and timber exports.
A regional stock exchange, the BVMAC, has had its headquarters in Libreville since a merger.
The Nkok zone was ranked the world's best SEZ for timber production by fDi Intelligence.
Fortescue signed an agreement to haul iron ore from the Belinga deposit to Owendo by combined road-rail.
The French military base at Camp de Gaulle was converted into a jointly run regional training academy.
